title: Psychoanalysis at the Edge of Recognition: Gaza and the Colonial Unconscious
abstract: Abstract This article examines the psychoanalytic implications of the destruction of Gaza through a qualitative, interpretive longitudinal analysis of the analytic work with a young Palestinian physician whose family and social world were devastated by war, displacement, and exile. Drawing on clinical material across successive phases of this experience, it argues that Gaza challenges psychoanalysis not only clinically but epistemologically. Under conditions in which the material and social foundations of everyday life are systematically dismantled, trauma can no longer be understood as a bounded individual psychic event, but emerges as continuous, collective, and historically situated. The paper explores the analyst’s position as witness and the limits of analytic neutrality when psychic suffering is inseparable from structural violence. Integrating psychoanalytic theory with decolonial thought, liberation psychology, and Palestinian‐centred scholarship, it develops the notion of a colonial unconscious to describe historical structures that differentially organize recognition within psychoanalytic discourse. The clinical material suggests that testimony can disrupt inherited interpretive frameworks while transforming the analyst’s own epistemic position. The article concludes that psychoanalysis may need to extend its frame beyond the dyad, allowing historical reality, collective memory, and plural forms of witnessing to participate in the analytic field.
